Title: Afghanistan Among World's Lowest in Academic Freedom, Scholars at Risk Report Shows

Summary: 
Afghanistan ranks among the world's lowest in academic freedom, scoring 0.08 on the Academic Freedom Index (AFi) according to the Scholars at Risk (SAR) 2025 Free to Think report released on October 1, 2025. The Taliban have intensified suppression of dissent: on December 1, 2024, Professor Hassamuddin Rahimzai of Sheikh Zayed University was beaten unconscious and detained after objecting to a faculty evaluation process favoring madrasa-trained loyalists. New restrictions required Afghan lecturers to obtain written approval from Taliban Supreme Leader Mullah Haibatullah to travel abroad for education or training. Ashley Rogers Berner of the Johns Hopkins Institute for Education Policy called the program 'mostly a positive thing,' citing 'choice plus academic accountability.' Meanwhile, national teachers unions like the NEA and AFT continue to oppose vouchers, arguing they weaken public school funding. However, a September 2025 poll found 73% of registered voters support open school choice, and only 20% would vote against a pro-choice candidate. Harvard improved from last place to 245th, partly due to defending campus groups targeted by the Trump administration; Stevens said, ‘I think the new president, President Garber, has been stronger on free speech than his predecessors.’ The study also found that 53 % of students view the Israel‑Hamas conflict as a difficult topic to discuss, and the 2024 presidential election was similarly challenging, while immigration was not seen as more difficult.

articles.title: USU free speech score drops amid Charlie Kirk controversy
articles.summary: Utah State University (USU) fell from 66th to 141st place in the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (FIRE) national free‑speech survey, receiving an overall score of 56.9 and an 'F' grade for speech climate. The drop coincides with controversy over a planned visit by conservative commentator Charlie Kirk, which was canceled after a campus debate and a petition. FIRE’s report, released on September 9, 2025, noted that 166 of 257 surveyed colleges received an 'F', while only 11 earned a 'C' or better. The survey of more than 68,000 students found that only 36% believe their administration clearly protects free expression, and a record one in three students said they accept some level of violence to stop speech. In the broader context, Claremont McKenna College topped the rankings, whereas Barnard College, Columbia University, and Indiana University were at the bottom. USU’s decline highlights the tension between its stated commitment to open dialogue and the fractured speech climate on campus, intensified by the fallout from Kirk’s canceled event.

articles.title: PM&DC Restores Passing Marks to 50 Percent for MBBS and BDS Students
articles.summary: The Pakistan Medical and Dental Council (PM&DC) has reversed its earlier decision to raise the passing marks for MBBS and BDS students from 50 percent to 65 percent for the 2024-2025 academic year. In a new notification issued on November 4, 2025, the council confirmed that the minimum passing score will return to the previous benchmark of 50 percent. This change follows widespread feedback from students and academic institutions opposing the higher threshold. Additionally, the council has reduced the required attendance for medical students from 85 percent to 75 percent. Universities and medical colleges have been instructed to implement these updated standards immediately. According to the PM&DC, the adjustments aim to create a more flexible and supportive environment, making medical education more accessible while maintaining quality standards for future healthcare professionals.

articles.title: Survey: College Students Show Declining Tolerance for Free Speech Despite Stated Support | Diverse: Issues In Higher Education
articles.summary: An American College Student Freedom, Progress and Flourishing Survey of 2,067 students at 472 U.S. colleges found that 74% say protecting free speech is more important than ensuring no one feels uncomfortable, yet 72% would report professors who say something offensive, a figure unchanged since 2021. Among 10 tested statements, 62% said professors should be reported for making one or more. Liberal (79%) and independent (74%) students were more likely than conservative (56%) to support reporting professors; female (81%) and other/unknown gender (84%) were more likely than male (57%). Support for disinviting speakers fell from 35% to 28%, dropping uncomfortable readings from 42% to 28%, and eliminating difficult topics from 31% to 23%. Still, 57% would report other students for offensive statements, slightly down from 62% in 2022. Only 43% believe the world has improved over the past 50 years, 23% are optimistic about the future, and 59% feel at least somewhat proud to be American. Regarding protest, 88% support peaceful protest, but 37% back occupying buildings, 23% disrupting classes, and 18% shouting down speakers. The average student spends 3.39 hours daily on social media, with 46% reporting negative mental‑health effects and 23% positive. The survey, conducted by College Pulse from June 23 to July 7, 2025, sampled 65% female, 30% male, 5% other; 52% liberal, 25% conservative, 23% independent. 'These findings do not suggest a campus environment open to the free inquiry and debate needed to advance knowledge and teach critical thinking,' the report concluded. 'As universities aim to enhance students' critical thinking skills and advance scientific knowledge, academic freedom and the ability to engage in a competition of ideas are essential to their missions,' said John Bitzan, lead researcher.

articles.title: Participation in Arkansas' school voucher program surges 157%
articles.summary: Participation in Arkansas' Education Freedom Accounts (EFA) school voucher program surged by 157% in its second year, rising from 5,548 students in 2023-24 to 14,256 in 2024-25, according to a University of Arkansas report. The program, which provides qualifying students with up to $6,994 annually for tuition, books, and other educational expenses, has seen 91% of recipients reenroll. The report projects that nearly 47,000 students—10% of Arkansas’s K-12 enrollment—will be approved for funding in 2025-26. Students in the program scored at the 57th percentile in math and 59th in English language arts, outperforming national averages. Of the 14,256 recipients, 76% (10,834) used funds at private schools, and 3,442 (24%) used them for homeschooling. The program disbursed $93.8 million, or 2.6% of the state’s K-12 education budget, despite serving only 3% of students. Notably, 36% of EFA recipients have disabilities—more than double the rate in public schools. Co-author Patrick Wolf stated the data 'dispels a lot of myths' about such programs. Ashley Rogers Berner of the Johns Hopkins Institute for Education Policy called the program 'mostly a positive thing,' citing 'choice plus academic accountability.' Meanwhile, national teachers unions like the NEA and AFT continue to oppose vouchers, arguing they weaken public school funding. However, a September 2025 poll found 73% of registered voters support open school choice, and only 20% would vote against a pro-choice candidate. Patrick Graff of the American Federation for Children praised the report as a 'treasure trove' of evidence supporting school choice, highlighting rapid growth, high retention, and strong academic outcomes.
